meta.title: Rip Currents: Preparedness and Prevention
meta.speaker: NOAA Ocean Podcast
meta.occasion: NOAA Ocean Podcast, episode 66 — Marissa Anderson with Dr. Gregory Dusek
meta.blurb: Rip currents kill more Americans most years than sharks, tornadoes and lightning combined — and the escape move is counter-intuitive.
meta.credit: NOAA Ocean Podcast, "Rip Currents: Preparedness and Prevention" (Episode 66). U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, National Ocean Service. Public domain (work of the U.S. Government).

summary.text:
Rip currents are seaward-directed jets of water that form in the surf zone of any beach with breaking waves — ocean coasts and the Great Lakes alike [1]. They rank ahead of tornadoes and lightning in U.S. deaths: about 100 drownings a year, third behind extreme heat and flooding [2]. Their speed can exceed five miles per hour — roughly the average speed of the men's 100-meter butterfly world record [3].

NOAA's answer is a forecast: a physical model of water levels and waves combined with a machine-learning model that outputs the likelihood of hazardous rips, roughly every mile of beach, every hour, up to six days out [4].

The survival core is counter-intuitive. A rip will not pull you under — it pulls you away from shore, so the first move is to relax and float [5], then swim out of the current along the beach and back at an angle. The best decision happens before you enter the water: swim near a lifeguard, where the odds of drowning drop to about 1 in 18 million [6].

concepts.definition: A narrow, fast, seaward-directed jet of water originating in the surf zone — 50 to 200 feet wide, reaching up to a quarter mile offshore.

cite.quote: rip currents can be, you know, anywhere from like 50 to 200 feet wide. They can go offshore to maybe a quarter mile or so in some cases, so they can go pretty far off the beach.

concepts.definition: The common name NOAA discourages: the phenomenon is a current, not a tide — something that pulls you from shore, not a rise of the sea.

cite.quote: It's not a tide, it's a current. It's something that pulls you from shore.

concepts.definition: A hybrid model — wave/water-level physics plus machine learning — that outputs hazard likelihood from 0 to 100%, like a precipitation forecast for the surf zone.

cite.quote: a machine learning model, which is kind of like a statistical model that predicts the likelihood of hazardous rip currents occurring from zero to 100%.

concepts.definition: The visual signature of a rip from an elevated viewpoint: a gap in the line of breaking waves, indicating a channel of deeper water.

cite.quote: Rip currents often occur in kind of flat spots in the line of breaking waves because that indicates deeper water.

flags.text: Before the beach: check the rip current forecast at weather.gov/beach.

cite.quote: And they can do that through weather.gov or going to weather.gov slash beach where they can find their particular weather forecast office and see the forecast there.

flags.text: Swim near a lifeguard — drowning odds fall to about 1 in 18 million.

cite.quote: Your chances of drowning at a lifeguarded beach are something like 1 in 18 million compared to an unguarded beach.

flags.text: If caught: don't fight it — swim out of the current along the beach, then back at an angle.

cite.quote: Swim out of the current along the beach so you're out of the current and then back to the beach at an angle.

flags.text: If you see someone caught: lifeguard first, else call 911; throw something that floats.

cite.quote: If you're not at a guarded beach, then you want to call 911 or have someone call 911

notes.text: Rip currents can move faster than an Olympic swimmer, and every year, lifeguards rescue tens of thousands of people in the U.S. who are caught in them.

notes.text: The counter-intuitive core: the current won't pull you under. Panic is the killer; floating is the escape.
notes.quote: as long as you can stay afloat, as long as you can stay on the water surface, you're going to be okay.
